clue.text: 19's profits

definitions.meaning: 19 across is the thrill or punt with the foot, and this is the footwear that delivers it
as an archaic verb, 'what does it avail?' was said with this word: it profits or benefits

explanation.surface: A cryptic cross-reference: the earnings of whatever 19 across turns out to be.
explanation.walkthrough: The 19 is a cross-reference to the 19-across answer, the thrill of starting a motorbike, i.e. a punt with the foot; footwear does that. The second sense is the old verb in 'what boots it?', meaning 'what good does it do?'
explanation.definitionFit: Footwear is what delivers a punt with the foot, and the archaic verb means avails or benefits.

clue.text: Artistic part of 1 ac's job

parts.note: 1 across is the hotel servant who polishes guests' footwear; the part of that job done with bristles is also a painter's handling of the paint

explanation.surface: The creative side of a hotel servant's daily round.
explanation.walkthrough: In old British hotels the 'boots' was the servant who cleaned guests' shoes, mostly with a brush; the same word names a painter's technique.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter's handling of the paint is called this, and a shoe-cleaner's work is literally done with bristled tools.

clue.text: How lofty its air !

parts.note: the instrument sits up in a church loft, and its tunes (airs) come from up there

explanation.surface: An exclamation at someone's haughty manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lofty air' reads as haughtiness, but the instrument lives in the church's loft and plays airs (tunes) from on high.
explanation.definitionFit: The church instrument with pipes is housed in a gallery called its loft, so its music literally comes from above.

clue.text: A phoney Gibraltar plant

parts.note: phoney means sham, fake
Gibraltar is known as the Rock

explanation.surface: A fake plant from Gibraltar.
explanation.walkthrough: Gibraltar, the British territory at the mouth of the Mediterranean, is nicknamed 'the Rock'.
explanation.definitionFit: The three-leaved clover is the national plant of Ireland, so it is a plant by example.

clue.text: Kept on singly or together by a good-tempered penitent

definitions.text: Kept on singly or together by a good-tempered penitent

parts.words: Kept on singly or together by a good-tempered penitent
parts.note: a calm person keeps the head's covering on and keeps the top garment on (both idioms for not losing one's temper); a penitent wears the two words joined as one garment

explanation.surface: Someone who stays calm while doing penance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep your hair on' and 'keep your shirt on' are British idioms for 'stay calm'; a good-tempered person keeps each on singly, and a penitent wears the two together as one coarse garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough garment of goat's fur worn against the skin was a traditional penance, a mortification worn by the repentant.

clue.text: Park murderer

definitions.meaning: a large royal park in central London
Mr ___ is the murderous other self of Dr Jekyll in Stevenson's story

explanation.surface: A killer in the park.
explanation.walkthrough: One word, two senses: a famous London park, and Dr Jekyll's violent alter ego in Robert Louis Stevenson's novella.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to London's best-known park and to the killer self of Stevenson's doctor.

clue.text: Favour may need cluing differently

indicators.note: arranged differently means the letters of the two words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A setter remarks that a clue might have to be written another way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'differently' shuffles NEED and CLUING together into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Granting a favour or allowance is a kindness, and in old use the word meant exactly a favour granted.

clue.text: Round Ronald this garment seems to droop

indicators.note: Round tells us the word for drooping goes around the name

parts.note: to droop is to sag
Ron is the short form of Ronald

explanation.surface: Ronald is wearing a garment that hangs loosely about him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' sits by 'Ronald', so it looks as though Ronald goes round something; in fact the drooping word goes round him, and 'seems to' is only padding.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrapped skirt-like cloth worn in South and South-East Asia is a garment.

clue.text: Rise in building material ? That's about right

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so the building phrase goes around the letter for right

parts.note: cement is a building material

explanation.surface: Is there a rise in the cost of building material? Yes, that's about right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts the building phrase around the letter for right, which lands after INC. 'Rise in building material' reads as a price rise; the definition is just 'Rise'.
explanation.definitionFit: A step-up or increase in amount, such as in salary, is a rise.

clue.text: End of the yarn of the unfinished drink

indicators.note: unfinished means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: rum is a drink

explanation.surface: Someone telling a tale while their drink sits half done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' cuts the last letter from THE, giving TH, then RUM. 'End of the yarn' sounds like the end of a story, but it is literal: loose thread ends left on a loom.
explanation.definitionFit: In weaving, the loose fringe of warp threads left on the loom after the cloth is cut off is this.

clue.text: Empty railway van is so open to attack

definitions.meaning: a guard's van with no guard in it is, read literally, without its guard

explanation.surface: An empty railway van is vulnerable.
explanation.walkthrough: British trains had a guard's van, where the guard rode; empty of its guard, it is literally 'un-guard-ed'.
explanation.definitionFit: A van lacking its guard is literally without one, and anything unprotected is exposed to attack.

clue.text: He hopes to come in first, for a certainty

definitions.note: a description of a person, standing for the noun: one who hopes to arrive ahead of the rest

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Someone confidently expects to arrive first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'come in first' reads as one phrase about winning, but 'in' is the hidden-word signal and the answer straddles 'for a certainty'.
explanation.definitionFit: A competitor in a race, horse or person, aims to finish ahead of the field.

clue.text: Cassius looked so like a hunter

definitions.text: Cassius looked so like a hunter

parts.words: Cassius looked so like a hunter
parts.note: in Julius Caesar, Cassius has 'a lean and ___ look'; a hunter out after prey looks that way too

explanation.surface: Cassius looked the part of a hunter.
explanation.walkthrough: The reference is Shakespeare's Julius Caesar: 'Yond Cassius has a lean and hungry look.'
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare gives Cassius a lean, famished look, and a hunter is driven by appetite for prey.

clue.text: It was a famous victory

parts.note: the 1704 battle won by Marlborough, recalled in Southey's poem with the refrain 'But 'twas a famous victory'

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a celebrated win.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes Robert Southey's poem 'After Blenheim', whose refrain is 'But 'twas a famous victory'.
explanation.definitionFit: Marlborough's 1704 battle in Bavaria is the victory Southey's poem names, with that line as its refrain.

clue.text: Article in packages unserviceable for the old physician

indicators.note: in tells us the article is placed inside the word for packages

parts.note: packages are parcels
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An item in damaged parcels destined for an old doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the article inside the packages, giving PARACELS. U/S, 'unserviceable', is British services slang for broken or useless.
explanation.definitionFit: The 16th-century Swiss doctor and alchemist is a famous physician of the past.

clue.text: Performs functions of piscine crews, say?

indicators.note: say means the phrase is spoken and its sound gives the answer

parts.note: piscine means fishy, and the crews of rowing boats are eights, so this is spoken as 'of fishy eights'

explanation.surface: Doing the job of a fishing boat's crew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' tells us to speak 'of fishy eights' (an eight being a rowing crew), which sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To act in an official capacity, as a referee or a priest does at a ceremony, is to carry out the duties of a role.

clue.text: Ace of suit has been misdealt — trying to be funny ?

indicators.note: cards misdealt are out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A card player complains that the ace was misdealt, and asks if someone is joking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misdealt' rearranges ACE OF SUIT into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Flippant, jokey remarks made at the wrong moment come from someone straining after humour.

clue.text: Look furtively both ways

indicators.note: the word reads the same forwards and backwards, so it works both ways

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Checking left and right before sneaking a look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'both ways' sounds like looking left and right, but means the word is a palindrome.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick sly glance, through a gap or keyhole, is a stealthy look.

clue.text: Ship's officer gets in tea, for cash

definitions.text: Ship's officer gets in tea, for cash

indicators.note: gets in tells us the word for tea is taken into the officer's title

parts.note: a purser is the ship's officer in charge of accounts
cha is British slang for tea

explanation.surface: The ship's accounts officer lays in tea and pays cash for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets in' reads as buying in stock, which is also the whole clue's picture: one who gets in supplies for cash. Cha is British slang for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A buyer is someone who acquires goods by paying money for them.

clue.text: One reeks badly of paraffin

indicators.note: badly signals the letters are put together wrongly, in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone smells strongly of lamp oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges ONE REEKS into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamp oil is called paraffin in Britain and by this name elsewhere, the same fuel.

clue.text: The thrill of starting a motorbike

definitions.meaning: a buzz or thrill of excitement
old motorbikes were started by stamping a lever with the foot

explanation.surface: The excitement of getting a motorbike going.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses: an exciting buzz, and the foot-stamp that starts an old motorcycle.
explanation.definitionFit: A buzz of excitement shares its name with the downward stamp of the foot on a motorcycle's starter lever.

clue.text: The city that is not united

definitions.text: The city that is not united

parts.words: The city that is not united
parts.note: the city's two football clubs are United and City, so the 'City' side is the one that is not United

explanation.surface: A town divided against itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not united' suggests a split town, but it is football: the city's clubs are United and City, and City is the one that is 'not United'.
explanation.definitionFit: The northern English city is home to both United and City football clubs.

clue.text: Change direction about two points, in a top coat

indicators.note: about here means around, so the turning word goes around the points

parts.note: to veer is to change direction
N and E are two compass points

explanation.surface: Advice to turn around between coats of paint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' sends the turning word around the two compass points, making VE-NE-ER. 'top coat' looks like an overcoat, but it is a surface layer on wood.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin decorative layer laid over cheaper wood is the outermost surface layer, so it is a top coat.

clue.text: As black and blue as the toad in the hole?

definitions.text: as the toad in the hole?
definitions.meaning: toad in the hole is sausages baked in a coating of batter

explanation.surface: Someone bruised like a creature stuck in a hole.
explanation.walkthrough: The held clue had 'road' for the scan's 'toad'. Toad in the hole is a British dish of sausages baked in Yorkshire pudding batter, so it is coated in batter.
explanation.definitionFit: A beaten person is bruised, and the British dish of sausages is cooked coated in batter.

clue.text: Van Tromp's Plantagenet emblem

definitions.meaning: the Dutch admiral Tromp was said to fly a brush from his masthead to show he would sweep the English from the sea
the dynasty took its name from planta genista, a yellow-flowered shrub, its emblem

explanation.surface: The badge of a Dutch admiral and an English royal house.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses: the sweeping brush the Dutch admiral Maarten Tromp is said to have hoisted, and the shrub (Latin planta genista) that gave the Plantagenet kings their name.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweeping brush and the yellow-flowered genista shrub share one name.

clue.text: Dr. Lake accepted infant sacrifices

definitions.note: a description (a verb phrase) of a deity, standing for the god himself

parts.note: MO, medical officer, is a doctor
a loch is a Scottish lake

explanation.surface: A doctor called Lake took in sacrificed babies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dr. Lake' reads as a person's name. The definition is a description: the Canaanite god to whom children were sacrificed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Canaanite deity in the Bible was worshipped with the burning of children as offerings.

clue.text: Oh, get round the airways to show you the magic of Africa

indicators.note: get round tells us the exclamation surrounds the airline's initials

parts.note: taken as written
BEA was British European Airways

explanation.surface: An exclamation about flying round to see African magic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get round' puts the exclamation around the initials of British European Airways, a former British airline. 'to show you' is padding.
explanation.definitionFit: Folk sorcery of West African origin, practised in the Caribbean, is a form of African magic.

clue.text: They measure up as top of the tips

definitions.note: singular phrase for a plural answer: these are tipsters' strongest selections

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a span, the width of a hand, is a measure

explanation.surface: Some tips prove worthy of the top rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses SPAN in this down entry. A 'nap' is a racing tipster's most confident selection of the day.
explanation.definitionFit: In British horse racing, a tipster's strongest selection of the day is called a nap.

clue.text: Belt round to, the first place where the air is bracing

indicators.note: the round letter is sent to the first position, ahead of the belt

parts.note: O is round in shape
a belt is a zone, as in a commuter belt

explanation.surface: A seaside resort with bracing air, the first one reached on a round trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to the first place' puts O before ZONE. The definition plays on the old belief that the bracing seaside air was rich in this gas.
explanation.definitionFit: Bracing seaside air was popularly said to be full of this form of oxygen.

clue.text: One can be uniformed without one being this

definitions.text: One can be uniformed without one being this

parts.words: One can be uniformed without one being this
parts.note: take the letter I (one) out of 'uniformed' and you get 'unformed', which means without form

explanation.surface: Someone may wear a uniform and still look a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'uniformed without one' as the word with its I (one) removed: UNFORMED, lacking shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Unformed means lacking definite form, the same as having no outline.

clue.text: Does not believe that damp in the air causes corrosion?

parts.note: mist is damp in the air
rusts means corrodes

explanation.surface: A doubter of the claim that humid air corrodes metal.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark reads as doubt, but the parts are MIST then RUSTS.
explanation.definitionFit: To doubt or suspect someone is to lack faith or trust in them.

clue.text: Blue anaesthetic

definitions.meaning: the blue sky, the upper air

explanation.surface: A blue knock-out drug.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses: the clear upper sky, poetically 'the blue', and an early anaesthetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Poets call the clear upper air of the sky by this name, and it was also an early surgical anaesthetic.
